tldr: This work achieves stable, high-precision humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation without retraining generalist VLA foundation models from scratch, combining kinematically grounded staged action generation (HAF-VLA) with frequency-compressed latent noise reinforcement learning (HAF-Steer).
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed Humanoid Adaptation Framework (HAF). Top: seven real-world tasks. Middle left: HAF-VLA, generating actions progressively from locomotion to dual arms. Bottom left: HAF-Steer, fine-tuning policies in a DCT-compressed latent noise space. As shown in the right plot, HAF significantly outperforms baseline methods.
overview:
To have humanoid robots carry out complex chores like household tasks, whole-body loco-manipulation is essential. The robot must tightly coordinate its foot locomotion, waist posture adjustment, and fine dual-arm manipulation. Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models that map camera images and language instructions directly to robot actions have gained significant attention. However, most existing models are designed for tabletop arms and predict all full-body degrees of freedom in a single shot. As a result, foot instability causes upper-body shaking, severely disrupting end-effector manipulation. Furthermore, policies trained solely via offline behavior cloning are fragile against real-world environmental shifts. At the same time, tuning massive VLA models directly with on-robot reinforcement learning (RL) is prohibitive due to heavy computational costs and serious safety risks.

To address these bottlenecks, the authors developed HAF (Humanoid Adaptation Framework), an adaptation framework transferring off-the-shelf flow-matching VLAs to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation. The framework consists of two complementary components. The first, HAF-VLA, leverages kinematic dependencies: it generates actions in three sequential stages, starting from locomotion and gaze, moving to waist posture, and finally dual-arm manipulation. By passing action feature caches from earlier stages, the robot manipulates objects with its hands on top of an already stabilized base. The second component, HAF-Steer, freezes the VLA backbone entirely and runs RL directly within the initial noise space from which generation begins. Using the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), it compresses temporal noise into just 8 low-frequency components, enabling safe and sample-efficient online adaptation while preventing jerky, unsafe real-robot behaviors.

Evaluated on two real humanoid platforms (TienKung 2.0 and 3.0) across seven household tasks, HAF boosted the average success score from 53.3% (achieved by a state-of-the-art single-stage VLA baseline) to 70.5%. Furthermore, additional adaptation via HAF-Steer demonstrated high task success even in out-of-distribution conditions where target table positions were shifted.
contributions: Proposed HAF, an integrated framework that efficiently adapts off-the-shelf generalist VLA foundation models to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation without retraining them from scratch.

Designed HAF-VLA, which generates actions hierarchically following kinematic dependencies across locomotion/gaze, waist posture, and dual-arm manipulation, enhancing coordination across lower and upper body joints.

Developed HAF-Steer, a latent offline-to-online RL pipeline leveraging flow-matching invertibility and Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to compress exploration into a compact low-frequency noise subspace, enabling safe on-robot policy refinement with a frozen VLA backbone.

Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance and robust generalizability over competitive baselines on two full-sized humanoid robots across seven long-horizon real-world tasks involving walking, bending, tossing, and carrying.

sections.heading: Why is humanoid whole-body coordination so challenging for generalist VLAs?
sections.summary: Humanoids couple locomotion, torso posture, and dual-arm manipulation, where any base instability corrupts end-effector precision. Generating all joints in a single step causes uncoordinated motions, and on-robot RL fine-tuning is impractical due to computational costs and safety hazards.
sections.details:
Unlike wheeled mobile manipulators or fixed-base robot arms, bipedal humanoid robots must coordinate foot locomotion, trunk/waist posture, and dual-arm manipulation with millisecond-level precision. If foot placement drifts even slightly, the upper body produces irregular compensatory motions to maintain balance, dramatically degrading hand manipulation accuracy.

Recently, generalist VLA foundation models pretrained on large-scale datasets (such as $\\pi_{0}$) have demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities. However, these models inherently generate all action dimensions simultaneously in a single shot. Predicting full-body actions without accounting for the kinematic dependencies between locomotion and manipulation frequently leads to disjointed, incoherent, and physically risky behaviors. Meanwhile, pretraining a humanoid-specific foundation model from scratch to resolve this would demand immense datasets and compute resources.

Moreover, a distribution shift between demonstration data and the real-world deployment environment is inevitable. Relying solely on offline behavior cloning (imitation learning) struggles to overcome these shifts, calling for fine-tuning via on-robot reinforcement learning (RL). However, directly updating a multi-billion-parameter VLA backbone with online RL is computationally prohibitive and poses severe safety risks of aggressive robot exploration causing hardware damage.

To resolve these challenges, this paper introduces the HAF framework, combining two complementary methods: HAF-VLA, which performs staged action generation aligned with physical kinematic hierarchies, and HAF-Steer, which safely runs RL within a compact latent noise subspace while keeping the pretrained flow-matching VLA frozen.

sections.heading: Where humanoid VLAs and latent RL stand today
sections.summary: Prior efforts have relied on humanoid-specific pretraining or full-parameter on-robot RL, facing data collection and safety barriers. Existing latent noise RL methods also struggle with either poor temporal expressiveness or overly large search spaces, both of which HAF overcomes.
sections.details:
This section reviews related work across three major areas, highlighting how the proposed framework differentiates itself:

- Humanoid VLAs: Robot foundation models originated in tabletop manipulation, but recent works like GR00T N1.7 and WholeBodyVLA have begun extending them to humanoids. However, these methods depend on massive pretraining on human video data or dedicated humanoid datasets. In contrast, this paper incorporates forward kinematic dependencies directly into the model architecture, transferring off-the-shelf generalist VLAs to humanoids without requiring massive new pretraining.

- Post-training VLAs with RL: Methods to improve imitation-learned policies include fine-tuning the entire model using algorithms like PPO or appending lightweight residual networks (Residual RL). However, full fine-tuning is computationally intensive and risks physical safety, while residual RL tends to accumulate temporal drift over long horizons. Optimizing the initial latent noise of diffusion or flow-matching models with RL has emerged as a promising alternative. Yet existing approaches like DSRL broadcast a single noise vector across the entire action chunk, severely sacrificing temporal expressiveness. Conversely, methods like UniSteer optimize noise across all timesteps independently, causing the search space to explode. HAF-Steer resolves this fundamental trade-off through spectral analysis.

- Whole-Body Manipulation Control: While low-level bipedal locomotion controllers trained with RL and VR teleoperation systems have progressed rapidly, they primarily serve as tracking controllers or data collection tools, lacking high-level language and visual reasoning within a unified hierarchical generative model.

sections.heading: HAF-VLA: Staged action generation aligned with physical kinematics
sections.summary: HAF-VLA decomposes the full-body action space into three sequential stages: locomotion/head, waist, and dual arms. Passing preceding actions as KV caches ensures foot stability while synthesizing precise, coordinated end-effector manipulation.
sections.details:
3.1 Hierarchical Full-Body Action Generation
A humanoid action chunk (prediction horizon $H=100$ steps, action dimension $D$ per step) is decomposed into four kinematically orthogonal components: locomotion and skill mode $a_t^{\\mathrm{move}}$, head posture $a_t^{\\mathrm{head}}$, waist posture $a_t^{\\mathrm{waist}}$, and dual-arm manipulation $a_t^{\\mathrm{manip}}$. Instead of generating all components in one shot, HAF-VLA predicts them progressively across three nested action sets with expanding action scopes:

- Stage 1: Determines the foundational base: locomotion, skill modes, and head (gaze) orientation ($\\mathcal{A}_t^1$).
- Stage 2: Adds waist joint commands to adjust trunk posture and establish the upper-body workspace ($\\mathcal{A}_t^2$).
- Stage 3: Fully activates all dimensions across the entire body, including dual-arm manipulation ($\\mathcal{A}_t^3$).

Crucially, earlier stage outputs are not frozen; rather, HAF-VLA employs cumulative inclusion ($\\mathcal{A}_t^1 \\subset \\mathcal{A}_t^2 \\subset \\mathcal{A}_t^3$), allowing later stages to refine previously sampled dimensions. This preserves full-body fluidity, such as making subtle foot adjustments in response to arm motions. To minimize computational overhead, visual and language features (Prefix KV cache $P_t$) are computed once and shared across all stages, and network weights are shared as well. Differentiating stage roles is achieved via learnable stage embeddings $e_s$ and action KV caches ($C_t^1, C_t^2$) encoding previous stage outputs as attention contexts. Only the final Stage 3 action chunk is sent to the robot controller.

3.2 Training Strategy and Deployment
During training, independent Gaussian noise and flow timesteps are sampled for each stage, and a masked flow-matching loss assigns zero target velocity to inactive dimensions. To prevent compounding errors during training, teacher forcing is used by encoding ground-truth actions into the action KV caches instead of intermediate model predictions. At inference time, each stage performs 10 denoising steps, totaling 30 steps across all three stages. A single RTX 5090 GPU completes inference in approximately 0.12 seconds, enabling real-time closed-loop control via receding horizon control (executing the first 40 of 100 predicted steps).

captions.F2: Model architecture of HAF-VLA. A shared action expert progressively expands generation from Stage 1 (locomotion & head) to Stage 2 (waist) and Stage 3 (dual arms). Clean action KV caches from earlier stages are passed to subsequent stages, and only the complete Stage 3 action chunk is dispatched to the robot controller.

sections.heading: HAF-Steer: Safe, lightweight online RL via spectral compression
sections.summary: HAF-Steer applies the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to compress the frozen VLA's initial noise space down to 8 low-frequency components, running Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) in this compact space. Because the VLA backbone remains frozen, it avoids hardware-damaging instability and acquires smooth real-world adaptation.
sections.details:
4.1 Spectral Latent Space Construction via Flow Inversion
Action generation in a flow-matching VLA is a deterministic mapping from initial noise $\\epsilon_t \\sim \\mathcal{N}(\\mathbf{0}, \\mathbf{I})$ integrated through the flow field. Steering this initial noise $\\epsilon_t$ can steer the output actions without modifying VLA backbone parameters $\\theta$. However, directly searching the raw noise space ($H \\times D$ dimensions, with horizon $H=100$) with RL leads to an excessively high-dimensional optimization problem.

To solve this, the authors apply a 1D Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) along the time horizon, retaining only the first $K=8$ low-frequency coefficients. Filtering out high-frequency noise components physically prevents high-frequency chatter and aggressive shaking during real-robot exploration. Additionally, by numerically integrating expert demonstrations $A_i^*$ backward through the frozen VLA flow field (flow reversal), corresponding expert initial noises $\\epsilon_i^*$ are recovered. Applying DCT and normalization yields offline expert spectral actions $z_i^*$.

4.2 Offline-to-Online Spectral Policy Learning
Policy learning proceeds in two phases:
- Behavior Cloning (BC) Initialization: A lightweight actor network $\\pi_\\psi(z \\mid x)$ is trained via regression on the expert spectral actions $z_i^*$ stored in an offline replay buffer.
- Mixed Offline-Online Reinforcement Learning: Following initialization, the robot collects transitions in an online replay buffer, updating the actor and critic using Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). Despite using a sparse success reward ($r=1$), keeping a BC regularization term on offline expert data prevents catastrophic policy collapse during early exploration. As online interaction progresses, the sampling ratio of offline data is gradually decayed to adapt the policy to deployment conditions.

4.3 Integration with Flow-Matching VLAs
When deployed with HAF-VLA, Stage 1 and Stage 2 execute standard sampling to build action caches, and HAF-Steer modulates only the initial noise of the final Stage 3. Because the VLA backbone remains completely frozen, computational overhead is exceptionally low.

captions.F3: Overview of HAF-Steer. (a) Standard VLAs denoise actions starting from random Gaussian noise. (b) HAF-Steer recovers initial noise from expert trajectories via flow reversal and compresses it into top-8 spectral coefficients using DCT. An RL actor is trained in this low-dimensional space and converted back into smooth noise via IDCT to guide the frozen VLA.

sections.heading: Real-humanoid household experiments across seven tasks and ablations
sections.summary: Using TienKung 2.0 and 3.0 humanoid robots, HAF was evaluated on seven long-horizon tasks including laundry loading and basket transfers. HAF-VLA substantially outperformed state-of-the-art baselines, and HAF-Steer online adaptation maintained high success even when tables were shifted to unfamiliar locations.
sections.details:
5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on full-sized humanoid robots, TienKung 2.0 and TienKung 3.0. Inputs consisted of a single head-mounted RGB camera stream and joint proprioception. Teleoperation data was gathered using an isomorphic system comprising a head IMU, dual master-slave arms, and joysticks for locomotion and waist posture (120 trajectories per task).
Seven household tasks were evaluated: Laundry Loading, Clothes Retrieval, Table Tidy, Basket Transfer, Toy Storage, Ball Tossing, and Box Transfer. Performance was measured by normalized task scores (%) reflecting milestone completion averaged over 10 trials.

5.2 Q1: Long-Horizon Task Performance (Table 1)
Baselines included ACT, $\\pi_{0.5}$, GR00T N1.7, and Cosmos Policy. HAF-VLA achieved the highest or tied-highest score across all seven tasks, reaching an average score of 70.5% compared to 53.3% for the strongest baseline ($\\pi_{0.5}$). The performance gap was particularly pronounced in tasks combining walking with precise manipulation, such as Box Transfer and Laundry Loading. In baseline models, hand poses drifted during base locomotion, leading to subsequent grasping failures.

5.3 Q2: Ablation Studies (Table 2)
Ablations on Laundry Loading validated the architectural choices. Comparing HAF-VLA against 'All-Joint Denoising' (denoising all joints simultaneously) and 'Arm-First Hierarchy' (predicting arms before base motion), the proposed 'Locomotion -> Waist -> Arms' sequence achieved the highest score. Attempting to determine arm motions first conflicted with base movement. Furthermore, allocating equal compute to $\\pi_{0.5}$ with 30 denoising steps degraded its performance due to inference latency, showing that hierarchical structuring provides inherent robustness to latency.

5.4 Q3: Robustness to Unseen Disturbances (Table 3, Figure 6)
In visual distractor tests (placing an unfamiliar black office chair along the walking path) and spatial perturbation tests (shifting the robot's initial position backward by 20 cm), HAF-VLA maintained high scores relative to $\\pi_{0.5}$, demonstrating resilient generalization.

5.5 Q4: Real-Robot Online Adaptation with HAF-Steer (Figure 7, Figure 8)
HAF-Steer was evaluated in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings, such as shifting the target table 30 cm farther than in demonstrations. DSRL, which broadcasts a single noise vector across time, caused severe robot jitter, forcing training to be aborted for safety. In contrast, HAF-Steer, restricted to 8 DCT components, safely completed on-robot RL and achieved substantially higher success rates than the Base Model or Noise BC. This confirms the complementary strengths of HAF-VLA's structured generation and HAF-Steer's latent adaptation.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: A new standard for whole-body humanoid VLAs
sections.summary: HAF combines hierarchical action flow generation with spectral latent reinforcement learning, providing a practical blueprint for adapting generalist VLAs to humanoid tasks. Future challenges include reducing inference latency and addressing base model expressive limits.
sections.details:
This paper presented HAF, a framework adapting pretrained generalist VLA models to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation. By generating actions across three kinematically grounded stages (HAF-VLA), it resolves upper-lower body coordination conflicts. Furthermore, by using DCT-compressed latent noise RL (HAF-Steer), it enables safe, lightweight on-robot adaptation while keeping the backbone model frozen.

The paper also transparently discusses several limitations:
- Increased Inference Latency: Executing three sequential stages increases the total number of denoising steps, which can impact closed-loop control latency (currently running at ~0.12 s per query on an RTX 5090).
- Dependence on Base Model Expressiveness: Because adaptation operates by steering initial latent noise, HAF cannot generate entirely novel behaviors or handle extreme edge cases that lie completely outside the frozen VLA backbone's representational capacity.

Future work aims to incorporate accelerated few-step denoising techniques and lightweight RL implementations to further enhance real-time responsiveness and physical robustness.

takeaways: Generating humanoid actions hierarchically along kinematic dependencies ('locomotion/gaze -> waist -> arms') drastically reduces upper-body drift and manipulation failures.
Using nested action sets instead of freezing earlier stage outputs allows later stages to adjust the entire body, which is critical for fluid full-body coordination.
In on-robot RL for large VLAs, compressing initial noise into low-frequency DCT components is a highly effective way to prevent violent hardware vibrations while bounding the exploration space.
Substantial real-robot performance gains can be achieved without retraining foundation models from scratch, simply through structured I/O hierarchies and lightweight latent-space RL.
limitations: Sequential multi-stage denoising increases computational burden and inference latency compared to single-stage generation methods.
Because the VLA backbone remains frozen and RL operates solely in latent noise space, acquiring entirely new behaviors absent from the base model's pretraining is difficult.
Real-world evaluations were confined to seven indoor household tasks; performance on outdoor irregular terrains and highly dynamic full-body motions remains unverified.
